displayQuote: Warriors of the light are not perfect. Their beauty lies in accepting this fact and still desiring to grow and to learn

meta.title: Who really said "Warriors of the light are not perfect. Their beauty lies in accepting this fact and still desiring to grow and to learn"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Paulo Coelho's Warrior of the Light, but the sentence is in neither the 1997 Portuguese original nor the English translation. A paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Warriors of the light are not perfect. Their beauty lies in accepting this fact and still desiring to grow and to learn'?
meta.ogDescription: Not in the book. Coelho's Warrior of the Light contains this sentence in neither Portuguese nor English - it is a later paraphrase of a real passage.

answer.label: Not Coelho’s wording — a paraphrase of his book
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Coelho’s, but the sentence is not. Every aggregator credits it to Warrior of the Light: A Manual (Manual do Guerreiro da Luz, 1997), yet a full-text search of that book turns it up in neither the Portuguese original nor Margaret Jull Costa’s English translation. What the book actually says is longer and plainer: warriors of light lie, betray, fail and hurt people they love, “and yet [have] never lost hope of being better.” The famous one-liner is a later compression of that passage by an unknown hand.

source.heading: The passage it was made from

docMeta.dd: Manual of the Warrior of Light
Margaret Jull Costa; English translation first published 2002 (HarperCollins)

source.excerpt: Every warrior of light has said ‘yes’ when he wanted to say ‘no’. Every warrior of light has hurt someone he loved. That is why he is a warrior of light, because he has been through all this and yet has never lost hope of being better than he is.
trail: Goodreads ↗ carries the line credited to “Warrior of the Light” and simultaneously warns that its quotes are community-added and unverified — the pattern behind most of the sourcing you will find for it.

Wikiquote ↗ files it under The Manual of the Warrior of Light (1997) with no page or chapter. Neighbouring bullets in that same list — “a warrior of light never confuses tension with anxiety,” for one — do check out against the book. This one does not.
The full text of the Jull Costa translation ↗, complete from the Luke 6:40 epigraph to the epilogue, contains no instance of “not perfect” or “beauty lies in accepting.”
Coelho’s own free web edition of the Portuguese original ↗ shows the same absence, so this is not a quirk of one translation. Quote Investigator has published no tracing of the line.
source.excerptNote: This is the closest the book comes, in Margaret Jull Costa’s translation. The popular quotation is a compression of it, not a sentence from it.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted for the popular sentence, because no source for it has been identified. Nothing about it is free to reuse by default: the work it is credited to is modern and protected — Manual do Guerreiro da Luz appeared in 1997, and the Internet Archive’s catalogue record ↗ dates Margaret Jull Costa’s English translation to 2002, so both the Portuguese text and the translation remain in copyright to Paulo Coelho and HarperCollins.

author.name: Paulo Coelho
author.kicker: The author it is credited to
author.heading: Paulo Coelho
author.bio: Paulo Coelho de Souza was born in Rio de Janeiro on 24 August 1947 and worked as a lyricist before turning to fiction; his 1988 novel The Alchemist became one of the best-selling books ever written. He has been a member of the Brazilian Academy of Letters ↗ since 2002. Several of his titles — Maktub, The Manual of the Warrior of Light, Like the Flowing River — are not novels at all but collections of essays and newspaper columns, which is part of why loose aphorisms attach themselves to his name so easily.

misattribution.heading: The name is right. The sentence is not.
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong author — it is a case of the wrong words. Coelho argued exactly this, at length; he just never wrote it like this, and the book he is said to have written it in does not contain it.

items.why: Aggregators are unanimous that the line comes from this book — Goodreads credits it to “Warrior of the Light” ↗ while carrying its own notice that community-added quotes are unverified. A search of the complete Jull Costa translation ↗ returns no hit for “not perfect” or “beauty lies in accepting.”
The absence is not a translation artefact. Coelho’s own free web edition of the Portuguese text ↗, complete from prologue to epilogue, contains no equivalent sentence either.

Wikiquote ↗ places the line as a bullet under its heading for The Manual of the Warrior of Light (1997) with no page or chapter reference, directly beneath the genuine passage it paraphrases — an arrangement that reads as corroboration and almost certainly hardened the false sourcing.

Two variants circulate, “Warriors of light” and “Warriors of the light,” and no attestation has been found that predates the quote-site era. Both read as condensations of the book’s litany rather than as anything a translator produced.

misattribution.truthLine: What Coelho actually wrote is better than the paraphrase: after listing every way a warrior of light fails, he concludes that this is precisely why he is one, “because he has been through all this and yet has never lost hope of being better than he is” — a passage Coelho still reprints on his own blog ↗.

context.heading: What the book actually argues
lead: Coelho really did build a book around the idea that his “warriors of light” are a mess. On his own blog he reprints the passage under the heading “What is a warrior of light?” ↗, credited to the Manual: they are often cowards, they don’t always act right, they suffer over useless things, they sometimes feel incapable of growing. That is the whole argument the popular one-liner is trying to summarise.

But summarising is exactly what happened. The book never states the thesis as an epigram; it accumulates it across a litany of confessions and lands on a single closing sentence. Somewhere between the page and the quote-card, that litany was boiled down to twenty-odd tidy words, and the tidy version — not the book’s — is what now travels under Coelho’s name.
context.detailsSummary: Why this book in particular collects phantom quotes
detailsBody: Manual do Guerreiro da Luz is not a narrative. Apart from the prologue and epilogue, the Portuguese Wikipedia entry ↗ notes that its contents had already been published in “Maktub,” a column Coelho ran in Folha de S.Paulo and other Brazilian and foreign newspapers between 1993 and 1996.

A book made of short, self-contained, unnumbered fragments is the ideal host for a fake: there is no plot to check a stray sentence against, no page a reader expects to be cited, and the register of the invention is indistinguishable from the register of the original. That is why the counterfeit sits so comfortably next to genuine lines such as “a warrior of light never confuses tension with anxiety,” which does appear in the translation.
context.pull: The book’s point survives the paraphrase. The sentence does not.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "Warriors of the light are not perfect. Their beauty lies in accepting this fact and still desiring to grow and to learn." as a bullet under the section heading for The Manual of the Warrior of Light (1997), with no page or chapter citation, immediately after the genuine "Every Warrior of the Light has hurt someone he loved" passage; the adjacent bullet "A warrior of the light never confuses tension with anxiety" is also listed.

This Internet Archive item holds the complete English text of The Manual of the Warrior of Light, title page reading "Translated from the Portuguese by Margaret Jull Costa", running from the Luke 6:40 epigraph through the Epilogue. A full-text search of it returns zero occurrences of "not perfect" and zero of "beauty lies in accepting", while "never confuses tension with anxiety" and "Every warrior of light has hurt someone he loved ... never lost hope of being better than he is" are both present.

The Internet Archive catalogue record for the HarperCollins edition gives publication date 2003, publisher "London : HarperCollins", the note "This translation originally published: 2002", and associated name "Costa, Margaret Jull".

This PDF is Paulo Coelho's own free web edition of the Portuguese original ("Edicao especial da pagina www.paulocoelho.com.br, venda proibida"), complete from Prologo to Epilogo. It contains no occurrence of "nao sao perfeitos" or "beleza esta em aceitar"; the nearest passage is the litany ending "Por isso e um guerreiro da luz; porque passou por tudo isso, e nao perdeu a esperanca de ser melhor do que era."

Paulo Coelho's official blog reprints "What is a warrior of light?", credited "in WARRIOR OF THE LIGHT: A MANUAL", including "They are often cowards. They don't always act right", "at times feel they are incapable of growing" and "have not lost the hope of becoming better". It does not contain the "not perfect / beauty lies in accepting" sentence.

The Portuguese Wikipedia article states that Manual do Guerreiro da Luz was released in 1997 and that, apart from the prologue and epilogue, its material had already been published in "Maktub", a column carried by Folha de S.Paulo and other Brazilian and foreign newspapers between 1993 and 1996.

The English Wikipedia article gives Paulo Coelho's birth as 24 August 1947 in Rio de Janeiro, describes him as a Brazilian lyricist and novelist and a member of the Brazilian Academy of Letters since 2002, and notes that Maktub, The Manual of the Warrior of Light and Like the Flowing River are collections of essays, newspaper columns or selected teachings.

Goodreads hosts the quotation "Warriors of light are not perfect.Their beauty lies in accepting this fact and still desiring to grow and to learn." credited to "Paulo Coelho, Warrior of the Light", above the site's own notice that quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.
